title: Vayera: visiting the sick (Genesis 18:1)
hookLine: God appears to Abraham as he heals; the rabbis learn that God visits the sick (Sotah 14a)
tomorrow: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly?

lines: GOD APPEARS AT THE TENT DOOR.
cards: When someone's sick, it can be hard to know what to do. What do you say? Will a visit intrude?

Maybe they want rest. So a text goes out instead: a heart emoji, get well soon. The fourth portion of the Torah opens with a single quiet verse: God appears to Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day.
It doesn't say why. But the rabbis looked at where this verse sits, right after Abraham's circumcision, and drew a conclusion that became a whole Jewish practice.

teach.h: AND THE LORD APPEARED UNTO HIM.
teach.b: The portion is called Vayera, and he appeared, from its first verse: "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." Why does God appear?
No message, no command. Just presence.
The rabbis noticed that the verse right before tells of Abraham's circumcision, at ninety-nine. So Abraham is recovering, sore, sitting in the shade.

teach.h: WALK AFTER GOD: CLOTHE, VISIT, COMFORT.
teach.b: The Talmud says God came to visit the sick, to ask after his welfare. Then it builds a whole teaching on it. The Torah says to walk after the LORD your God.
How can a person walk after God? By copying God's ways. God clothed the naked, Adam and Eve; so you clothe the naked.
God visited the sick, Abraham; so you visit the sick. God comforted mourners, Isaac after his father died; so you comfort mourners. God buried the dead, Moses; so you bury the dead.

The Hebrew for visiting the sick is bikur cholim: bikur, a visit, and cholim, the sick. It's a mitzvah, a commandment, and some Jewish communities have a bikur cholim group whose whole job is to show up.
The Talmud even says a visitor takes away a small part of the illness, one sixtieth. It's not medicine. It's company.
The rabbis give the visitor practical advice too: don't sit up high over the sick person; sit at their level. And they expect a visitor to ask for mercy for the one who is sick.
Just by showing up, the rabbis say, a visitor does what God did at a tent door on a hot day.

how: Visiting the sick is a mitzvah in Jewish law; some synagogues have bikur cholim volunteers who visit hospitals and homes, and the Mi Sheberach prayer for healing is said during the Torah reading.

o: visiting the sick, a mitzvah learned from God
a prayer for healing said at the Torah reading
a hospital chaplain's blessing at the bedside

games.q: walking after God — tap the pairs.

s: Genesis 18:1 says why God appeared to Abraham
the verse gives no reason; the rabbis read it from its place after the circumcision.
the Talmud says a visitor takes away one sixtieth of the illness
bikur cholim is only a nice custom, not a commandment
it's a mitzvah, learned from walking in God's ways.

games.q: a friend is recovering from surgery. you're not sure they want company. what does the Jewish teaching suggest?
o: send a text and stay away.
visit, briefly, and sit at their level.
games.why: show up, and sit at their level, not over them. that's bikur cholim, and it's what God did at the tent door.

practice: Think of someone who's sick, hurting or recovering, near or far, and picture yourself sitting beside them, at their level, not standing over them. You don't need to say anything clever; just be there.
If you pray, ask for their healing; if you don't, hold them in mind with warmth.

wordCard.voice: Bikur cholim. Visiting the sick: a Jewish commandment learned from God, who appeared to Abraham as he healed.

carryVoice: Your line: visit the sick. Not a text: your voice, or your face. Day one hundred seventy-six.
